catalog_quote: The remaining vocabularies are based on lists compiled by students at the Methodist Goldie College, Banga Island, New Georgia, except for Kia, which was gathered by the present writer. The only points of spelling that need to be referred to are: (1) the plosives b and ḍ are always prenasalised, except in Kia; (2) g is a velar fricative /γ/ while (3) stress is very frequently ante-penultimate. Any stress that would cause difficulty in interpretation will be marked by an acute accent as in some of the language names above.

new_statements.rule_in_words: A blanket transcription note covering all of Capell's 100-item vocabularies (six Choiseul varieties including 'Vagua' = Vaghua, plus New Georgia languages, Mono and Kia): stress is said to fall very frequently on the antepenultimate syllable, with any interpretively troublesome stress to be marked by an acute accent; no acute accents appear on the Vagua items. It is NOT a Vaghua-specific description and gives no default-vs-exception rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Only that non-obvious stresses would be marked with an acute accent (none visible on Vagua entries in the text layer).
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms in student-compiled Swadesh-type wordlists; group-level remark for Choiseul/New Georgia/Mono/Kia lists as a whole, not verified for Vaghua. Note the nearest described relative, Sisiqa (Ross 2002:457-458), is described as penult-default with an antepenult class of echo-vowel words, so Capell's 'very frequently ante-penultimate' cannot be read as a fixed rule for Vaghua.
new_statements.identity_note: Capell 1968's 'Vagua' list and Tryon & Hackman's list 4 'Vaghua' are the target language (vagh1249, ISO tva); older names for the same area are Tavula/Tavola, Tambatamba (Capell 1943), Tarikukuri/Tabataba, Kunabena/Bota and Liuliu (Lanyon-Orgill 1950; all cross-referenced to VAGHUA in Tryon & Hackman 1983). The quoted Capell sentence is NOT specific to Vaghua: it covers all his Choiseul, New Georgia, Mono and Kia vocabularies. Nearest relative with a published stress rule is Sisiqa (sisi1250; Ross 2002:457, penult default) -- a different language of central Choiseul; closest sister Varisi (vari1239) is likewise undescribed.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The reader listed only one work, and it was opened and read, so there were no listed silent or not-opened works to spot-check. I spot-checked instead the other works held by the project that marks silent: (1) Lanyon-Orgill 1950, Anthropos 45:57-58 ( lines 3805-3860): the introduction gives only the alphabet and consonant values (b = mb, d = nd, j = nj/nz, g hard, ng, ngg), no stress or accent remark, and no accent glyphs in the vocabulary region (lines 3800-9100); (2) Capell 1943, Oceania 14:21 ( lines 1559-1600): 'Babatana (phonetically mba'mbatana)' and stress ticks on Varese 'kunzuku, Ririo 'kunjuku and 'pupuku, Sengga and Kirunggela 'popuku, but no tick on any Tambatamba (= Vaghua) item…
